points.description: The answer conveys the purpose: both reverse path methods make broadcasting more efficient than flooding by reducing duplicate packets in the network.

The answer conveys how Reverse Path Forwarding works: a node forwards a packet from source S only if it arrived over the neighbour the node would itself use to route back to S (its unicast routing table's best route), and it forwards to all other neighbours but not back to the sender.
points.partial_credit: Half marks if the answer states the arrive-on-best-route check but omits that the packet is not sent back to the incoming neighbour, or vice versa.

points.description: The answer conveys how Reverse Path Broadcast works: nodes learn from observed unicast traffic which links lie on spanning trees they belong to, and they forward broadcast packets only on those tree edges (still applying the reverse-path check and not sending back to the incoming neighbour).
points.partial_credit: Half marks if the answer says RPB only forwards on spanning-tree edges without explaining how nodes learn those edges from unicast traffic, or explains the learning without the tree-edge restriction.

rubric.notes: Full marks require the efficiency purpose, the RPF rule (forward only if the packet arrived over the neighbour used to reach the source, not back to that sender), and the RPB extension (forward only on spanning-tree edges learned from unicast traffic). Points P2 and P3 carry most of the mark because they explain how the methods work. Equivalent wording and alternative correct explanations earn the marks.
